body_markdown:
Richard Bond, now 85, fell in love at first glimpse. Said this longstanding Hagerty member: “At a local show in 1997, photos of a ’47 Studebaker pickup in the back of a fellow’s car are what sparked my interest. The exterior design and the Stude’s gorgeous paint convinced me that this truck was well worth pursuing, in spite of the fact I already owned a ’41 Willys pickup.


“During several months that followed, I tracked this pickup through three successive owners. I finally found it in October of 1997, in Riverview, Michigan, 20 or so miles from my Belleville residence.


“Incredibly, not one penny changed hands to move this Studebaker to my garage! The owner happily traded it even-up for the nice ‘35 Plymouth 5-window coupe I owned at the time.”


Don Sherman


Don Sherman


Don Sherman


Don Sherman


Bond retired in 2008 after his stint at the Ford Motor Company’s research and engineering center in Dearborn, where he specialized in cold weather testing that was conducted in the lab. For three decades, he’s been a member of the National Street Rod Association and the Goodguys Rod & Custom Association. Quite naturally he associated with a dozen or so[Studebaker fans](https://www.hagerty.com/media/opinion/against-all-oddities/always-itching-for-more-studebakers/) in his clubs because of the ’77 Avanti II he owned for years.


Studebaker got its start producing electric delivery vehicles in 1902, followed by gas-powered cars two years later. Many historians call 1925 through 1940 the firm’s “golden age,” during which it competed quite well against other U.S. makers. During World War II, Studebaker was contracted to supply military trucks and aircraft engines.


When hostilities ended, Studebaker’s slogan became “first by far with a post-war car.” Thanks to the company’s accomplished designers Virgil Exner and[Raymond Loewy](https://www.hagerty.com/media/magazine-features/hagerty-magazine/from-russia-with-loewy-failed-world-car/) , its cars and trucks were more aerodynamic than the competition offered, and they were equipped with forward-reaching “wind wing” door vent windows.


Don Sherman


The M-series pickup trucks built from 1941 through 1948 were highly successful, with 67,809 delivered in 1947 alone. Unfortunately, Studebaker’s 1954 merger with Packard was catastrophic. Truck production ended in 1964, and the last Studebaker car left the assembly line in ‘66.


During the first half of its life, Bond’s ’47 pickup was significantly upgraded by successive owners. A small-block V-8 engine, a three-speed Hydramatic transmission, independent front suspension, and disc brakes from a Chevy Monte Carlo were installed. That upgrade included power steering, power brakes, and a tilt steering column. Bumpers were stripped, running boards were streamlined, and bucket seats were added. The gorgeous purple paint that seized Bond’s attention was applied by one of the earlier owners.


Don Sherman


Don Sherman


Bond’s stewardship began three years ago, and he has been busy. Under the hood, he added a chrome air cleaner and valve covers with blue accents, and a “Pecker Power” cowl cover. Factory exhaust manifolds were replaced with more efficient headers, and a new aluminum radiator was installed. His sweeping dash is now loaded with a full array of gauges from Classic Instruments. The cargo bed floor was rebuilt with magnificent hardwood panels. He also installed power-operated struts to open his hinged bed cover.


Don Sherman


Don Sherman


Don Sherman


Don Sherman


Bond added strips of purple running lights under the doors and cowl, at the end of the bed, and underneath the dashboard. The tiny fuel cell that came with the car was replaced by a 15-gallon fuel tank filled through the bed floor. Motor City Solutions of Taylor, Michigan, pitched in when necessary.


Bond explains, “All my effort was aimed at making my pickup roadworthy because I intended to drive it often to car shows and club events. I replaced the tires with fresh Sumitomo radials mounted on Weld polished-aluminum wheels. Averaging 500 or so miles per year, I’ve logged at least 15,000 reliable miles in this pickup.”


Bond’s face lights up the instant his barely muffled V-8 fires with a twist of the ignition key. “It’s a little loud,” he exclaims, “just the way I like it!”
